title: A Bill to Give AI an Emergency 'Kill Switch'
hook: A bipartisan bill would let a US agency order AI companies to hit the brakes — shut a system down or throttle it. It's still just a proposal, but it puts a government 'off switch' on the table.
key_points: The proposed 'AI Kill Switch Act' would let the Department of Homeland Security order companies to shut down or throttle AI systems.
It's bipartisan — Reps. Ted Lieu (D-CA) and Nathaniel Moran (R-TX) were set to introduce it, Politico reported via The Verge.
The idea: give the government an emergency brake if an AI system is judged a serious threat.
It's only a proposal — not law, and a long way from any vote.
A 'kill switch' is easy to picture but hard to build: modern AI runs across many machines and can be copied.
content_html: Lawmakers are floating a literal off switch for AI. According to a Politico report relayed by The Verge, Reps. Ted Lieu (D-CA) and Nathaniel Moran (R-TX) were preparing to introduce an "AI Kill Switch Act" — a bill that would let the Department of Homeland Security order AI companies to shut down or throttle their systems.
extra_html: The pitch is an emergency brake: if an AI system were judged a serious threat, the government could force the company running it to power it down or slow it to a crawl. The proposal is notably bipartisan, with a Democrat and a Republican named as sponsors — a sign that unease about powerful AI crosses party lines. But it's worth keeping the stage in mind: this is a proposed bill, not a law, and it has a long road through Congress before anything takes effect. It's also a reminder that a "kill switch" is far easier to picture than to build. Modern AI doesn't live on one computer you can unplug — it runs across many machines and can be copied — so an orderly, reliable shutdown is a genuinely hard technical problem, not just a policy one. For now the story is about intent: a growing appetite among lawmakers to hold an emergency lever over the technology.

related.title: Rules & Regulation
related.hook: AI raced ahead of the law, and governments are now scrambling to catch up. The big debate: how to curb real harms without strangling a genuinely useful technology.

related.title: Who Controls AI?
related.hook: The most powerful AI models are built by a handful of giant companies, because training them costs a fortune. Who holds that power — and whether 'open' AI can balance it — shapes everything.

related.title: Will AI Take Over?
related.hook: The Terminator scenario — AI 'waking up' and turning on us — isn't what serious researchers worry about. Their real concerns are more mundane and more immediate.

flashcards.prompt: What would the proposed 'AI Kill Switch Act' let the government do?

choices.text: Order AI companies to shut down or throttle systems judged a serious threat
Ban all AI chatbots in the United States
Require every AI answer to be fact-checked before you see it

flashcards.explanation_html: The bill would give the Department of Homeland Security authority to order companies to power down or throttle an AI system — an emergency brake, not a blanket ban.

flashcards.prompt: Is the 'AI Kill Switch Act' a law you have to follow?
flashcards.back_html: No. It's a proposed bill that lawmakers were set to introduce — not law, and a long way from any vote. Proposals often change or die before becoming rules.

flashcards.prompt: Why is an AI 'kill switch' easier to imagine than to build?
flashcards.back_html: Modern AI systems run across many machines and can be copied, so there's rarely a single plug to pull — shutting one down cleanly is harder than it sounds.
